title: Dalton's Law Partial Pressure Infographic
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: AP Chemistry
description: Interactive infographic for Dalton's law of partial pressures. Sliders set the moles of three gases and the total pressure; flask pictures, a pie chart of mole fractions, and a table of moles, mole fractions, and partial pressures update together.

learningObjectives: Calculate the mole fraction and partial pressure of each gas in a mixture
Verify that the partial pressures of the gases in a mixture add up to the total pressure
standards: AP Chemistry CED Unit 3, Topic 3.4: Ideal Gas Law (partial pressures and mole fractions)

controls.label: Gas A
controls.description: Moles of gas A, 0.5 to 3.0 mol in steps of 0.1

controls.label: Gas B
controls.description: Moles of gas B, 0.5 to 3.0 mol in steps of 0.1

controls.label: Gas C
controls.description: Moles of gas C, 0.5 to 3.0 mol in steps of 0.1

controls.label: Total P
controls.description: Total pressure of the mixture, 0.50 to 2.00 atm in steps of 0.05

assumptions: Ideal gases that do not react with one another
All four flasks have the same volume and temperature, so dot count is proportional to pressure (40 dots per atm)

keyQuestions: How is the mixture flask related to the three single-gas flasks?
Why does adding more of gas A lower the partial pressures of B and C when the total pressure is held constant?
commonMisconceptions: Believing heavier or larger gas molecules exert a larger share of the pressure
Confusing mole fraction with partial pressure when the total pressure is not 1 atm
Forgetting that mole fractions must add up to 1
assessmentOpportunities: Have students calculate mole fractions and partial pressures on paper, then verify with the MicroSim
